content:
Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has moved from asking whether feedback works to asking how learners engage with it. This review synthesises what the project library establishes about uptake, attention, and affective response across teacher-provided, peer-provided, and automated feedback, treating engagement as the mechanism that conditions whether feedback translates into revision.

Liu and Wu (2019) found that students preferred teacher feedback and direct correction with metalinguistic explanations, with preferences varying by proficiency. Mao et al. (2024) reported that over half of the surveyed teachers experienced negative emotions when providing WCF. Koltovskaia (2022) reported that teachers provided feedback on both higher- and lower-order concerns despite Grammarly's presence, with no division of labour, although the hypothetical, one-time design limits claims about sustained practice.

Zhang and Hyland (2018) showed that engagement with AWE varied sharply between learners, and Hyland (2025) cautions that much research occurs outside naturalistic contexts, raising questions about classroom applicability. Luo et al. (2025) found that ChatGPT's error detection improved substantially with prompt sophistication, overtaking Grammarly in recall while remaining highly precise.

Peer feedback shows a parallel pattern: Li and Hébert (2023) reported that all students incorporated support-related peer feedback and that paper ratings improved significantly between drafts (d = 1.62), yet some students ignored unity- and word-use-related comments.

Affective and motivational responses are increasingly treated as outcomes in their own right. Razmi and Ghane (2024) found that direct unfocused WCF raised writing self-efficacy and reduced anxiety relative to a control group, but the exclusively male, intermediate-level sample limits generalisation. Teng and Ma (2024) found that feedback-related strategies in participation were the strongest predictor of academic writing performance among 708 Chinese EFL learners, though the self-report design constrains inference.

quotes: Overall, the majority of respondents (42/70, 60%) preferred feedback given by teachers.

One overriding finding is that students at all proficiency levels preferred teachers’ guidance in error identification and correction, and none expressed faith in relying on peers as the sole source of feedback.
In general, students favored direct correction in conjunction with metalinguistic explanations (215/447, 48.10%) followed by direct correction without metalinguistic explanations (111/447, 24.83%).
Overall, students preferred direct correction accompanied by metalinguistic explanations.
It is also clear from this study that proficiency plays an intricate role in how students view feedback and its impact on learning.
It is clear that students’ reliance on teachers as an exclusive source of feedback declined as their proficiency increased.
As shown in Figure 7, Level 6 differed from the other three levels in that students at this level generally preferred error coding (20/41, 48.78%) to the three other types of CF.

verifications.explanation: The claim's central proposition — that engagement with AWE feedback differed sharply between learners — is supported. The source states that "The differences between their engagement types became more obvious in their responses to AWE feedback when there was a multiple drafting opportunity" and that "It is clear that the two students engaged with teacher and AWE feedback on their writing differently." The contrast is documented concretely: Flora "resubmitted her essay 13 times" and "was fully engaged behaviorally with the revision task," whereas David "only resubmitted his essay once after receiving AWE feedback and only spent less than 14 minutes on the task," showing "a low level of behavioral engagement with AWE feedback." The peripheral assertion about the learner population (two Chinese case-study students) is also supported. No assertion is contradicted and no hedge is removed.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has moved from asking whether feedback works to asking how learners engage with it.

This review synthesises what the project library establishes about uptake, attention, and affective response across teacher-provided, peer-provided, and automated feedback, treating engagement as the mechanism that conditions whether feedback translates into revision.
Teacher feedback remains the default preference.
Automated writing evaluation (AWE) is treated as a complement rather than a replacement.
Affective and motivational responses are increasingly treated as outcomes in their own right.
What is established is that feedback type shapes immediate accuracy and that engagement varies by learner.
What remains contested is whether these gains persist, and whether AWE can support rhetorical development rather than surface correction alone.
